case_source: (From the Judgment an Order dated 20th August passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3869 of 2000)
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J:- This appeal by leave arises out the judgment and order dated 21.08.2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3869 of 2000 making the Rule absolute declaring that the orders dated 01.11.98 passed in Title Suit Nos. 7,9,10,11,13,14 and 15 of 1998 of the Court of District Judge, Dhaka have been passed without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect and also directing the Court of District Judge, Dhaka to dispose of the above suits from the stages as those were on 01.11.98 strictly in accordance with the provisions of Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure as quickly as possible.

2. The respondent No. 1, as plaintiff, along with Title Suit Nos. 8 and 12 of 1998, also filed the Title Suit Nos. 7,9,10,11,13,14 and 15 of 1998 in the Court of the District Judge Dhaka, (Court) against the defendant appellant bank under Order 37 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) stating inter alia that they drew 9 Bills of Exchange (Bills) for a total sum of Tk. 1,02,70.000,00 drawn on Bangladesh Agricultural Department Corporation (BADC) during the years 1985-87 under Letter of Credit No. 001-003-85 (Local) dated 20.01.1985 (L/C) issued and confirmed by the appellant and the appellant, though accepted for honor the above Bills, neither issued a notice of dishonor nor caused to note protest for dishonor by non-accepted of any of the above Bills and thereby Continued to remain to be the holder without consideration thereof and the cause  of action in Title Suit Nos. 8,9,11 of 1998 arose after the appellant under his latter No. DIL/SOD/78/97 dated 23.7.97 denied haying "accepted for honor" the said 9 Bills and cause of action in Title Suit Nos. 7,12,13,14 and 15 of 1998 arose after the appellant by its letter No. NBL/DIL/RW/505/ 97 dated 18.09.1997 admitted to have dishonored 9 Bills by non payment and in view of above the respondent No. 1 drew 9 Bills of Exchange on 15.9.97 and 25.5.97 for a total sum of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 including therein a sum of  Tk. 8,24,67,069.00 which accrued as interest and also Tk. 79,24,92,446.00 which became due as compensation under section 117 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881(Act).

3. In Title Suit No. 7 of 1998 the respondent No. 1 prayed for decree of Tk. 10,60,13,047.00 and also for further interest and compensation on the above decrial amount stating inter alia that against the 2nd bill dated 2.5.1985 drawn by them for a  sum of Tk. 9,96,190.00 a sum of Tk. 93.65,450.00 accrued as interest from 17.5.1985 to 16.8.1997 @ 5% per quarter and again on the above total sum of Tk. 1,03,61,640.00, (Principal Tk. 9,96,190.00  Interest Tk. 93,65,450.00) further sum of Tk. 9,56,51,407.00 became due as compensation @ 10% per quarter from 17.5.1985 unto 16.8.1997 under section 117 of the Act. In similar way, respondent No. 1, in Title Suit No. 8 of 1998 prayer for decree of Tk. 3,78,72,580.00 against 6 Bill dated 4.5.1986 for a sum of Tk. 5,05,068.00  claiming Tk. 38.84,105.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 3,34,83,407.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 9 of 1998 prayed decree of Tk. 19,59,756.00 against 7 Bills dated 31.7.1986 for a sum of Tk. 25,67,500.00 claiming Tk. 1,97,93,569,00 as interest thereon and Tk. 17,36,14,687.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 10 of 1998 prayed for decree of Tk. 17,29,93,645.00 against 81. Bill dated 4.10.1986 for a sum of 24,95,610.00 claiming Tk. 1,81,47,860.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 15,23,50,179.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 11 of 1998 prayed5 for decree of Tk. 16,61,363.00 against 91 Bill dated 22.1.07 for a sum of Tk. 26,720.00 claiming Tk. 1,81,821.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 14,52,824.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 12 of 1998 prayed for decree of Tk. 11, 70,09,222.00 against 4th Bill dated 29.6.1985 for a sum of Tk.10,03,163.00 claiming Tk. 99,52,714.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 10,60,53,345.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998 prayed for decree of Tk.12,08,16,577.00 against 3rd Bill dated 10.6.1985 for a sum of Tk. 10.27,000.00 claiming Tk. 1,02,89,209.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 10,96,00,368.00 as compensation thereon and in Title Suit No. 14 of 1998 prayed for decree 5th Tk. 11,08,21,887.00 against 5th Bill dated 30.10.1985 for a sum of Tk.10,41,378.00 calming Tk. 97,90,90,275.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 9,99,90,234.00 as compensation thereon and in. Title Suit No. 15 of 1998 prayed for decree of Tk. 12,73,71,110.00 against 1st Bill dated 19.10.1985 for a sum of Tk. 9,96,190.00 claiming Tk. 1,04,27,518.00 as interest thereon and Tk. 11,59,47,402.00 as compensation thereon.

4. Thus in the above 9 suits the respondent No. 1 against 9 Bills drawn on BADC during the years 1985-87 for total sum of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00, sought decree for Tk. 99,05,35,187.00, which is nearly 100 times more than Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 the total amount of the 9 Bills, on the ground that since those Bills for total amount of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 were dishonored the respondent No. 1 drew subsequent 9 Bills dated 15.9.57 and 25.9.97 for a sum of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 which became due in view of dishonor of earlier 9 Bills as in the meantime a sum of Tk. 8,24,67,069.00 accrued as interest on Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 and a sum of Tk. 79,24,92,446.00 also 1 became due as compensation on the above  amount of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 as compensation, Further in the above suits over and above the amount of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00, the respondent No. 1 also claimed further interest on the decrial amount.

5. In the paper book only the order sheet. of Title Suit No. 7 of 1998 has been furnished which shows that since requisite court fee of Tk. 28,750.00 for each suit was  not filed along with the aforesaid 9 applications (plaints) filed on 25.1.98, the Court  without registering those suits fixed different dates for heating those on the matter of court fees as well as maintainability and on  19.7.98, the date fixed, the respondent No. like previous date, was also found absent but even then the court accepted the suits provisionally subject to final decision regarding court fees and maintainability  and ordered for issuing summons upon the  defendant appellant fixing next date on  24.8.98 for return and the summons having  returned, the court by order dated 24.8.98 fixed the next date on 13.9.98 for filing written objection and hearing but in the meantime on 26.8.98, the appellant entered appearance and prayed for time to file written statement and then on 30.8.98 the appellant also filed another application supported  by affidavit praying for leave to appear and defend the suit contending inter alia that they received the summons only on 19.8.98 and there is a defence to the suit and m such  it is reasonable that hey should be allowed to appear and defend the suit and the Court then fixed the next date on 11.10.98 for  hearing of the above application. However on 13.9.98 the respondent No. 1 filed an application praying for passing an order to the effect that the appellant defaulted in obtaining leave of the court to appear and defend. The Court then fixed the next date on 11.10.98 for hearing both the applications dated 30.8.98 and 13.9.98 and on 11.1.98 those were taken up for hearing but during hearing none was present on behalf of the plaintiff respondent No.1 and the court, after hearing, by order dated 1.11.1998 granted leave, relevant portion of which is as follows: -

"It is further submitted by the learned Advocate that the defendant Bank on 26.8.98 i. e. On the 8th day of service of summons has entered appearance along with an application praying for time to file written statement to defend the suit and time was allowed fixing date 13.9.98 for filing written statement, but due to bonfire mistake and inadvertence by the conducting advocate the said application was not supported by affidavit stating the grounds of defence with a formal prayer for leave to appear and to defend the suit and to cure the said defect the defendant Bank is filing the present petition duly supported by affidavit stating the grounds of defence of the suit with a formal prayer for leave to appear and to defend the suit. It is further submitted by the learned Advocate that the present suit is false, fraudulent, frivolous and malafide one and it has been filed by suppression and concealment of facts regarding filing of Money Suit No. 22 of 1980 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Court No.1 Dhaka subsequently on transfer renumbered as Money Suit No. 16 of 1987 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Court No. 2, Dhaka and obtaining an exparte decree and thereafter filing of execution of the said exparte decree and dismissal of the said execution case. It is further stated that the issuance of the Bills of Exchange and the calculating of interest and compensation are on the face is illegal, arbitrary, fanciful, baseless and not entertain able and therefore, the defendant Bank is legally entitled to leave to appear and to defend this suit is In support of this submission learned Advocate has cited a decision reported in AIR 1953 Madras 909 where it is found that a court has power in a proper case before the passing of decree, to grant leave to defend the suit even though the defendant has not applied for leave within 101 days of the service of summons. I have carefully gone through the petition under order 37 rule 3 of the Code and the case record where it is found that tribal issue has been raised and thereafter, the defendant Bank should be allowed to appear and to defendant the suit.

6. As it appears the respondent No. 1 then filed Civil Revision No. 10 of 1999 before the High Court Division challenging the orders dated 1.11.89 passed only in Title Suit Nos. 8 and 12 of 1998 whereupon Rule was issued on 5.1.1999 but in July 2000, inspite of pendency of above Rule, the respondent No.1, filed writ petition No. 3869 of 2000 challenging the same very orders dated 1.11.98 passed in the remaining Title Suit Nos. 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 of 1998 and more so therein the respondent No. 1 prayed for issuing Rule only upon the Presiding Judge of Dhaka District Court, Dhaka, who was made the respondent No.1, though it is the appellant who was to be affected in case the Rule in above writ petition was made absolute. In the above writ petition it was contended, inter alia, that the information slips showed that summons of the above suits were served on the appellant on 19.8.1998 but the appellant did not file any application under rule 2(2) or under Rule 3 of Order 37 CPC for obtaining leave and that against the orders dated 1.11.98 they filed applications dated 7.11.99 under section 152 CPC praying for amendment of the errors made in the said orders dated 1.11.98 but those were illegally rejected by the Court. The High Court Division then on 23.7.2000 issued Rule only upon the respondent No. 1 i. e. the Presiding Judge of the District Court, Dhaka to show cause and the respondent No.1 having not appeared, the High Court Division after hearing only the respondent No.1, though found that the appellant, having received the summons on 19.8.98 and 28.9.98 as well as 29.8.98 being holidays the application dated 30.8.98 is within 10 days, but made the Rule absolute on the ground that the above application dated 30.8.1998 did not disclose a tribal issue. The relevant portion of the above judgment is as follows:

"Summons of the suits were served upon the defendant Bank on 19.8.98 under the law a defendant in such a case is to obtain leave to appear and defend within 10 days from the service of the summons upon him, 28th and 29th August were respectively Friday and Saturday and as such the defendant filed applications in each of the suits on 30.8.98 within the time under Order 37 Rule 3 CPC praying for leave to enter appearance and to defendant the suits District Court Judges can only grant a defendant leave to appear defend the suit if the defendant raises a triable issue, but we find that the paragraph as quoted above did not contain any Bible issue. Leave to defend should be granted if there is an arguable defence and a case is put forward which a court will have to enquire into and come to a decision. But if the alleged defence is illusory, sham or bogus one then leave to defend should be refused. However where the learned Judge find himself in a genuine doubt as to whether the defence is genuine or not he can grant leave only on certain conditions."

Leave was granted in the following terms:

The High Court Division erred in law in not considering that the last part of Rules 3(1) of Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure provides "or such other facts as the Court may deem sufficient to support the application." Which means this part gives discretion to the learned District Judge to deem it sufficient; the Court shall give leave to appear and to defend this suit. Accordingly the learned District Judge upon perusal of the application filed by the appellant Bank and upon hearing the appellant Bank to file the suit since the Bills of Exchange appeared to be not drawn on the petitioner Bank. Since the learned Judge deemed the facts sufficient to support the application the teamed Court did not act without lawful authority in granting leave to the petitioner Bank to appear and to defend the suits."

7. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant submits that the words " or such other facts as court may deem sufficient to support the application "as contain in rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC means that if other facts, apart from the facts disclosed in the affidavit, are sufficient for giving leave, the court has the discretion to grant leave to appear and defend the suit ; in the present suits the contents of the applications dated 30.8.98, the submissions of the learned advocate of the defendant appellant and the case records show that the respondent No.1 in respect of this very transaction obtained exparte decree against the appellant in Money Suit No. 16 of 1987and then filed Money Execution Case No.242 of 1991 but the above execution case was dismissed from the contents of the averments made in the applications (plaints) of the above suits it will appear that Bills for total sum of Tk.1,02,70,000.00, in respect of which cause of action of the above suits arose, were drawn by the respondent No.1 during 1985-87 on BADC and not on the appellant and then the respondent No.1 alleging that those Bills were dishonored drew 9 Bills on the appellant for a total sum of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 on 15.9.98 and 25.9.98 i.e. after a period of 10/12 years which is long beyond the period of limitation as provided in Article 64A of Limitation Act ; in case of alleged dishonor of the Bills drawn on BADC during 1985-87 as alleged, subsequent Bills dated 15.9.97 and 25.9.97 should have been drawn on BADC which was enclosed with the letter dated 18.9.97 on which the respondent No.1 relied for the cause of actions of the suits, show that BADC, against total claim of Tk. 1, 02,70,000.00 in respect of 9 Bills which are against the value of spare parts made payment of Tk. 85,28,372.32 after dedicating Tk. 17,41,627.68 as penalty etc. as per terms of the contract and then the respondent No. 1 challenging the above deduction instituted Miscellaneous (Arbitration ) Case No.1011 of 1992 in the Court of 3ra subordinate Judge Dhaka for appointment of an arbitrator to resolve this dispute and after hearing the Court vide order No. 32 dated 15.01.96 appointed and Arbitrator and vide order No.33 dated 30.01.96 also directed the Arbitrator to start proceedings but against that above orders BADC filed Civil Revision No.1130 of 1996 before the High Court Division and obtained rule as well as order of stay and thus it is evident that the claim of the respondent No.1 is against BADC and not against the appellant and the actual claim relates to in respect of deduction of Tk. 17,41,627.68 from the Bills as penalty etc. and the dispute as to whether Tk. 17, 41, 627. 68 were legally deducted is pending before the High Court Division for decision; the respondent No.1 has filed the present suits only with the intention of defeating the claim of the appellant as will be evident from the fact that the appellant on 10.3.98 instituted Title Suit No. 13 of 1998 in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.3 Dhaka against the respondent No.1 for recovery of Tk. 1,57,53, 570.13 only and before filing of the suit the appellant served notice dated 18.09.97 upon the respondent No.1 and upon receipt of the above notice dated 18.09.97 the respondent No.1 in order to defeat the realization of the legitimate dues of the appellant in Title Suit No. 13 of 1998, instituted the instant suits on 25.01.98; in the such summery proceeding under Rule 2(2) (a) of Order 37 CPC respondent No.1 is only entitled to claim interest as specifically provided in sections 79 or 80 of the Act and not any compensations as claimed in the present suits under section 117 of the Act which represents about 80% of the amount for which decree was sought the appellant being not at all connected with the above deduction of Tk. 17,41,627,68 the respondent No.1 had no basis to draw 9 Bills of Exchange dated 15.9.97and 25.9.97 for an amount of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 on the appellant and more so when those bills were also not accepted by the appellant. The learned counsel next submits that in paragraph 5 of Title Suit Nos. 8 and 11 it has been stated that statement of Account No. SOD-539 furnished on 8.7.97 showed that opt of 9 Bills of Exchange 1st, 2nd, and 3rd were fully honored and 4th and 5th were and the remaining 6th, 8th and 9th remained dishonored and so as per the above the respondent No. 1 can not Take any claim whatsoever against 1st, 2nd and 3rd Bills and cannot also claim the full amount against 4th and 5th Bills; further along with the letter dated 18.9.97 on which the respondent No.1 relied for causes of action for the suits the certificate dated 13.12.88 issued by BADC was enclosed, which op the other hand showed that 1st, 2nd, 3rd & 4th Bills Exchange out of which Title Suit Nos. 7th, 13th, and 15th of 1998 arose, were fully honored and against the remaining 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th, out of which Title Suits Nos. 8, 9,10, 11,12 and 14 of 1998,only Tk. 17,41,627.85 was deducted from the total Bill amount of Tk.1,02,70,000.00 but the respondent No.1 in the above suits claimed, total amount of Tk. 102,07,000.00 due against the 9 Bills drawn on BADC during 1985-87; the court, granted leave specifically mentioning the submission of the learned advocate of the defendant (appellant) to the effect that " issuance of the Bills of Exchange and the calculation of interest on the face of it is illegal arbitrary, fanciful, baseless and not entertainable" but the High Court Division not only failed to take into consideration the above position but also failed to take into consideration the fact as to who was the person likely to be affected in case the Rule was made absolute just following the prayer as made in the writ petition by the respondent No.1 with malafide motive, issued Rule only upon the presiding Judge, District Court Dhaka, the respondent No.1, fully being aware of the fact that such judges being merely formal party, do not appear not to speak of contesting the Rule and thereby the High Court Division, falling in the trap set up by the respondent No.1 not only issued Rule only upon the writ respondent No.1 but also made the Rule absolute just within 28 days from the date of the issuance of the Rule depriving the appellant the opportunity to oppose the Rule and disclose facts as stated above and thus enabling the respondent No. 1 to obtain decree for Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 even without paying any Court fee as yet the High Court Division also failed to consider that there was inordinate delay in filing the writ petition and that applications under section 152C.P.C. as mentioned in the writ petition were filed by the respondent No.1 only on 7.11.99, after more than one year from the respondent No.1 only on 7.11.99, after more than one year from the date of passing of the order dated 1.11. 98 by availing the equally efficacious remedy the respondent No.1 filed Civil Revision No. 10 of 1999 under Section 115(1) C.P.C. only against orders dated 1.11.98 passed in Title Suit Nos. 8 and 12 of 1998 whereupon Rule was issued and during pendency of the above Rule, the respondent No.1 with ulterior motive filed the above writ petition suppressing the fact of issuance of Rule in the above Civil Revision No. 10 of 1999 and the pendency thereof and that subsequently after hearing the above Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 10 of 1999 was discharged on merit affirming the order dated 1.11.98 granting leave to the appellant to appear and defendant the suit.

8. The constituted attorney of the respondent No.1, who appeared in person, submits that 10 days time having expired before filing application dated 30.8.98 the learned District Judge had no power to extend the time in view of the provision of Article 158 If Limitation Act, as is evident from the contents of the information sleep, the applications filed on 30.8.98 were under Rule 2(2) and not under Rule 3 of Order 37 CPC and further in the said applications dated 30.8.98 though supported by affidavit the appellant prayed for leave to appear and defend the suit merely stating therein that there is defence to the suit on merit but without disclosing any ground of and so the respondent No.1 on 13.9.98 filed an application praying for passing an order to the effect that the defendant appellant defaulted in obtaining leave of the Court as the court for granting leave cannot take any other fact into consideration except those disclosed in the applications dated 30.8.98 and in the case of hived Traders vs. Premer Soap Factory Ltd. 44 DLR 490 the High Court Division affirmed this position as is evident from the letter of the appellant dated 18.9.97 and the certificate of BADC dated 13.12.1988 money was admittedly due against 9 Bills drawn during the years 1985-87 and so the respondent No. 1 drew fresh 9 Bills for Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 on 15.9.97 and 25.9.97 for the amount which became due in the meantime due to addition of interest and compensation and those remaining unpaid the respondent No. 1 filed the present suits but the court completely ignoring the provisions of Rule 3 of Order 37 CPC granted leave to the appellant; in terms of L/C dated 20.1.85 9 Bills were drawn on BADC during 1985-87 and the Statement of Account dated 11.3.99 issued by the appellant and the certificate dated 13.12.88 issued by BADC will show that the appellant collected payments on the proceeds thereof to the Account of the respondent No.1 and accordingly the appellant, having collected payments on the Bills of Exchange is trustee for the respondent No. 1 and so in the present case a trust having been created, section 10 of the Limitation Act 1908 will apply in accordingly as held in 12 DLR 10, limitation will not run the dismissal of Money Execution Case No. 241 of 1991 for execution of the exparte decree obtained by the respondent No. 1 in Money suit No. 16 of 1989 has no nexus to the filing of the present suits and no inordinate delay was also made in the filing the writ petition because in the meantime on 7.11.99, the respondent No.1 filed application under section 152 CPC for amendment of the order dated 1.11.98 but with no result and as held in PLD 1978 SC 96 holder of such a Bill must be able to obtain a judgment as early as possible and so the respondent No.1 was entitled to invoke the writ jurisdiction for speedy relief and further, on 23.5.2000 i.e before filing of the writ petition the respondent No.1 duly served on the District Judge, Dhaka notice demanding justice.

9. The point for consideration is whether in view of the words "or such other facts as the court may deem sufficient to support the application as contain in Rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC the learned District Judge was entitled to grant leave in the present case though the contents of application dated 30.8.1998, which was supported by affidavit, did not disclose sufficient facts as would make it incumbent on the holder of the bill to prove consideration, Rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC provides as follows:

"3-(1) The Court Shall, upon application by the defendant, give leave to appear and to defendant, the suit upon affidavits which disclose such facts as would make it incumbent on the holder to prove consideration, or such other facts as the Court may deem sufficient to support the application."

10. As it appears the word "or" after the words "upon affidavit which discloses such facts as would make it incumbent on the holder to prove consideration as above makes the above words and the words such other facts as the court may deem sufficient to support the application disjunctive. The first part of Rule 3(1) above refers facts which have been disclosed in the affidavit whereas the later part refers to the facts which the Court may find from the case records or otherwise in support of the application for leave even though these facts have not been disclosed in the application affirmed by affidavit.

11. It may be mentioned here that since the provisions of Order 37 CPC is summery one and is a departure from the procedure provided for in ordinary suits and further since Rule 3(1) of Order 37 laid down some stringent conditions for granting leave, in AIR 1953 Madras 909, madras High Court initially gave some relief regarding limits lion wherein it was laid down that Court has power in a proper case before the passing of decree, to grant leave to defend the suit even though the defendant has not applied for leave within the prescribed period of the service of summons upon him. Earlier in the case of S. Murahair Rao vs. K. Bapayya AIR 1949 Madras 742 Mack J. also held that the court has jurisdiction to condone delay and given leave even if the application for leave to defend has not been made within the prescribed period of limitation and he further held that it is not necessary that every procedural order of a court should be supported by a specific statutory provision, and when there is neither provisions nor prohibition it has to be guided by ordinary principles of common sense, justice, equity and good conscience."

12. But these two authorities were not considered as good law in the case of Shah Mohamed Khan V. H. N. Wood fall (S) AIR 1955 Mad 637 wherein it was held that a court has no power to condone the delay in filing the application under 0.37 r. 3 Civil P.C. as S.5 of the Limitation Act has not been made applicable to it. Section 3 of the Limitation Act is mandatory, and when the application is filed beyond the time prescribed by Art. 159 it must be dismissed.

13. However in the case of Kishan Singh Vs. Md. Shaif AIR 1964 Jammu & Kashmir 39 this question of limitation came up for consideration wherein the Court considering the provisions of Rule 4 of Order 37 CPC took different view holding as follows:

"8. The Division Bench authority of the Madras High Court, (S) AIR 1955 Mad 637 (Supra) is based on a reading of S.5 and Art 159 of the Limitation Act. On a deeper analysis of the provisions of 0.37 of the Civil P.C. this authority appears to be not only harsh and too technical but ignores the other provisions of 0.37 r. 4 of this order (which) empowers a court under special circumstances to set aside a decree passed by the Court under he provisions of this order, and further empowers it to grant leave to the defendant to appear and defend the suit. A case can be envisaged wherein here exist special circumstances within the meaning of this rule which would satisfy a Judge to set aside the decree and allow the defendant to defend the suit under the provisions of R.4, But if (S) AIR 1955 Mad 637 (Supra) is followed strictly, it means that the same set of special circumstances, when brought to the notice of the Court under the provisions of R.2 are to be rejected, because the application for leave to defend is not presented within the period limitation prescribed therefore. The Judge being, therefore, powerless, has to pass a decree as envisaged by O. 37, R. 2 After passing the decree on the same set of facts, he can set aside the decree and grant the visions of existing law nugatory would look not only anomalous, but should even go to the length of saying ridiculous, and would result only in duplication of work and waste of time of the court and the parties. If the court has power to allow the defendant to get a decree set aside in the special circumstances disclosed by him to the satisfaction of the court under R.4 and be permitted to defend the suit, this power should be considered inherent in the court while disposing of his application for leave to defend under the provisions of R. 12, Otherwise, pass a decree, and then on the basis of the same circumstances set aside the decree and allow the defendant to defend the suit.

14. It is a cardinal Principle of interpretation of statues that when two provisions of a statue appear conflicting with each other they should be so interpreted so that they harmonies. (See Pajkrushna Bose V. Binod Kanugo AIR 1954 SC 202. In another authority of the Supreme Court reported as Babulal Bhuramal V. Nandram Shivram, AIR 1958 SC 677 their Lordships have laid down that:

"If it is possible to avoid a conflict between the provisions of different sections of the same Act on a proper construction thereof, then it is the duty of a court to so construe them that they are in harmony with each other."

Similarly if is well settled that if two constructions are possible, the court must adopt that which will implement and which ensures the smooth and harmonious working of the Act or the Rule and discarded that which will stultify the apparent intention, and therefore, eschew the other which leads to absurdity or gives rise to practical inconvenience of makes well established provisions of existing law nugatory-------

(13) Lord Herschel in Colquhoun v. Brooks, (1889) 14 AC 493 at P. 506 observed.

"It is beyond dispute That we are entitled and indeed bound when construing the terms of any provisions found in a statute to consider any other parts of the Act which throw light upon the intention of the legislature and which may serve to show that the particular provision ought not to be construed as it would be if considered alone and apart from the rest of the Act."

(14) In another case Cox v. Hakes, (1890) 15 AC 506 at P. 529 the same learned Judge held-

"It cannot, I think, be denied that, for the purpose of construing any enactment, it is right to look not only at the provision immediately under construction, but on any others found in' connection with it, which may throw light upon it and afford an indication that general words employed in it were not intended to be applied without some limitation."

(15) In the Light of these observations when we interpret the provisions of O.37 we have to so interpret them the as would lead to a harmonious construction of the entire order and avoid results which would result in absurdities and make one provision of the Act conflict with the other.

(16) In any view therefore, as already stated, the special circumstances which would entitled me to set aside a decree under the provisions of R.4 would at the same time empower me to give leave to defend the suit, even if the application is beyond give leave to defend the suit, even if the application is beyond time if the special circumstances mentioned by the petitioner are convincing".

15. According considering the interpretation as given to Rule 3(1) and 4 of Order 37 CPC in AIR 1964 J & K 39 in paragraph 16, the words or such other facts as the Court may deem sufficient to support the application as provided in Rule 3(1) above should not be restricted by the words upon affidavits which disclose such facts as would make it incumbent on the holder to prove consideration" as in many cases for fault of the lawyers, as in the present case, application seeking leave even supported by affidavit may not contain facts disclosing trouble issue and accordingly we are of the view that the court in the present case was entitled to give leave because of he words or such other facts as the court may deem sufficient to support the application as contained in Rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC.

16. In this context it may be mentioned that in the case of Mr. Komarmal Gurudayal Vs. Sagarmal Bengani, A.I.R 1972 Cal. 430 it also held that though indolence may not be an excuse to constitute sufficient cause, mistake of law not accompanied by negligence or inaction may be considered as sufficient causes. In the present case as it appears the learned District Judge considered the fact that a client should not suffer for the bonfire mistake of the lawyers.

17. In respect of the question as to under what circumstances leave to appear and defend is to be given to the defendant Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Fine Textile Mills Ltd Vs. Haji Umar P.L.D S.C. 1963 at page 163 held as follows:

"Where the defendant discloses upon his affidavits facts which may constitute a plausible defence or even show that there is some substantial question of fact or law which needs to be tried or investigated into, then he is entitled to leave to defend. What is more is that even if the defence set up be vague or unsatisfactory or there be a doubt as to the genuineness, leave should not be refused altogether but the defendant should be put on terms either to furnish security or to deposit the amount claimed in Court. The principles upon which the provisions of Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil procedure 1908 should be applied are not dissimilar to the principles which govern the judgment in a suit filed by a specially endorsed writ of summons under order XIV of the Rules of the Supreme Court in England. One of such principles laid down by the Court of Appeal is that at the stage when leave to defend is sought "the Judge is not to try the action he is to see that there is a bona fide allegation of tribal issue, which is not illusory he need not be satisfied that the defence will succeed it is enough that such a plausible defence is verified by affidavit."

18. Accordingly in the present suits the court, even if the defence set up in the application dated 30.8.98 was vague or unsatisfactory, could grant leave and the only scope left to the respondent No.1 was to raise the objection that the application was not put in terms either by furnishing security or by depositing the amount claimed in the Court.

19. Now coming to the question whether there was a triable issue, the present suits arose out of 9 Bills drawn on BADC during the years 1985-87 copies of which have been furnished in the paper book. As it appears in the above 9 Bills the respondent No.1 gave order to BADC to pay total sum of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00. In the L/C dated 20.1.85, which has been furnished in the concise statement, it has been specifically provided that interest if any, has to be paid by BADC. As is evident from the contents of the paper book in paragraph 5 of the applications (plaints) of Title Suit Nos. 8 and 11 of 1998 the respondent No. 1 categorically   stated that the Statement of Account No. SOD —539 furnished on 8.07.1997 show that out of the 9 Bills of Exchange accepted for honor, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Bills of itching were honored in full and the 4th and 5th were lion oared in part and the 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th of bills of exchange were dishonored by non payment and accordingly on that basis there are no causes of action for filing Title Suit  Nos. 15, 7 and 13 of 1998 as those arose out of 1st, 2nd and 3rd Bills of exchange drawn on 19.3.85, 2.5.87 and 10.6.85 respectively as those were honored in full and in the like manner in Title Suit Nos. 12 and 14 of 1998, which arose out of 4th and 5th Bills of Exchange drawn on 29.6.85 and 30.10.95 respectively, full amount as above suits not only the full amount due against the Bills were claimed, but also interest under sections 79 and 80 as well as compensation under section 117 of the Act on the full amount of the bills were claimed.

20. It further appears that in applications (plaints) Title Suit Nos. 7, 12, 13, 14 and 15 the respondent No. 1 categorically stated that cause of action of the above suits arose as appellant in letter No. NBL/DIL/RW/505/97 dated 18.9.97 categorically admitted to have "dishonored by payment" of all the 9 Bills of Exchange. In the remaining Title Suit Nos. 8, 9and 11 of 1998 in the applications (plaints) the respondent No. 1 also categorically stated that cause of action of the above suit arose as the appellant in letter No. Dil/ SOD/ 78/97 dated 23.07.97 denied having "accepted for honor" the 9 Bills of Exchange. Since the copy of the plaint of Title Suit No. 10 of 1998 is not in the paper book the particulars of the cause of action of the above suit could not be ascertained. The copy of the letter dated 23.7.98 could not be found in the Paper Book but however from the contents of the above letter No. NBL/DIL/RW/505/97 dated 18.9.97 which has been famished in the concise statement, it appears that the above letter dated 18.9.97 was issued with reference to the earlier letter dated 23.7.97 issued by the appellant by which the appellant requested the respondent No. 1 to adjust the outstanding loan and that since loan was not adjusted in-spite of the letter dated 23.7.97, the appellant, by the above letter dated 18.9.97 requested the respondent No.1 to adjust the entire outstanding of Tk. 1,57,53,570,43 as on 30.6.1997 In the said letter the photocopy of the certificate dated 13.12.88 of BADC, which issued against the request letter of the respondent No.1 dated 3.12.88 and which was sent to the appellant by the respondent No. 1 was also enclosed. The above certificate dated 13.12.88 shows that respondent No.1 drew the above 9 Bills during 1985-87 total value being Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 to BADC under L/C No. 001-003-85 (Local) dated 20.1.85 against which total sum of Tk. 85,28,372,.32 was paid by BADC to respondent No. 1 deducting an amount of Tk. 17.41,627.68 from the Bills as penalty etc. as per terms of the contract and , as submitted by the learned counsel of the appellant, the respondent No.1 raising the grounds that such deductions are breach of the terms of the contract, filed Miscellaneous (Arbitration) Case No. 1011 of 1992 in the Court of 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dhaka (Now 3rd Joint District Judge), challenging such deduction and the above court appointed arbitrator for resolving the dispute and being aggrieved the appellant filed Civil Revision No. 1130 of 1996 in which Rule was issued and order of stay was passed and the Rule is pending for hearing.

21. Further the letter dated 18.9.97 and the certificate dated 13.12.88 issued by BADC on which the respondent No.1 practically relied for the cause of action for all the suits, show that the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Bills of Exchange were fully honored and it is only from the 5th, 6th, 7th and 9th Bills total sum of Tk. 17,41,627.68 was deducted as penalty etc. as per terms of the contract. However as stated earlier in paragraph 5 of the plaint of Title Suit Nos. 8 and 11 of 1998 the respondent No.1 stated that out of the Bills of Exchange 1st, 2nd and 3rd were honored in full and 4th and 5th were honored in part. So there is apparent contradiction in the claim of the respondent No.1 In any view of the matter, in terms of the stand taken for the causes of action Title Suit Nos. 7, 12, 13, 15 of 1998 which arose out of 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th Bills could not at all be filed as the connected Bills were fully honored and the remaining Title suit Nos. 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14 of 1998 which arose out of the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th Bills of exchange could be filed only claiming Tk. 17,41,627. 68 in total, which was deducted from the above Bills and as stated earlier the question as to such deduction of TK. 17,41,627.68 is pending before the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1011 of 1992. it also appears that the respondent No. 1 filed Money Suit No. 16 of 1987 (previously 22 of 1980) against the appellant calming from them Tk. 1,57,33,570.43 for realising arrears against supply to spare parts to BADC which was decreed exparte and thereafter the respondent No.1 filed by filing Money Execution Case No. 241 of 1991 prayed for execution of the said decree but the above execution case was dismissed and the respondent No.1 did not above execution case was dismissed and he respondent No.1 did not challenge the above order of dismissal.

22. It further appears from the case records that the appellant filed Title Suit No. 13 of 1998 in the Court of Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 3 Dhaka on 10.3.98 against the respondent No. 1 for recovery of Tk. 1.57, 53,570.43 only and before filing of the above suit the appellant served legal notice dated 18.9.97 upon the respondent No.1 and on receipt of the said notice, the respondent No.1, instead of adjusting the claim as demanded, drew on the appellant 9 Bills, of Exchange on 15.9.97 and 25.9.97 claiming total Tk. 99.05,3,187.00 claiming that 9 bills of Exchange drawn on BADC during 1985-87 were dishonored but as stated earlier BADC in whose name Bills of Exchange were drawn during 1985-87 made payment against those bills and for the amount of Tk. 17.41.627.68 deducted by BADC from the total amount of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 litigation is pending and the claim of the appellant is that they never accepted the above Bills drawn on 15.9.98 and 25.9.98. Moreover those being drawn on the 10-12 years after alleged dishonor, is barred by limitation under section 64A of the Limitation Act.

23. Further in terms of the condition of the letter of credit dated 20.1.85 interest, if any, has to be paid by BADC and further in terms of Rule 2(2)(a) of Order 37 CPC, on the amount remaining unpaid against the Bills of Exchange, which in the present case appears to be Tk. 17,41,627.68 the respondent No. 1 could charge interest only under sections 79 and 80 of the Act and there was no scope calming compensation under the Act as in the present suits as Rule 2(2) above did not keep any provision for claiming compensation under section 117 of the Act but as it appears in the present suits the respondent No.1 not only claimed entire amount of the 9 Bills of Exchange drawn on BADC during 1985-87 i.e Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 but also claimed Tk. 8,24,67,069.00 as interest on the amount of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 and apart from the above also claimed Tk. 79,24,92,446.00 i.e. about 80% of the suit amount, as compensation under section 117 of the Act. Accordingly on the face of it, the claims as made in the application (plaints) of the above suits, have no basis whatsoever and accordingly the court found force in the submission of the learned advocate of the defendant (appellant) to the effect that the claims in the suits are illegal, arbitrary fanciful and not entertainable.

<u>24. It also appears that considering the situation which arose in view of the Order 37 providing for filling special kind of suit and special procedure for an adjudication and also considering many instances in which application could not be filed within time, in many states of India, by amendments, provisions have been made either allowing applications under section 5 of the Limitation Act or giving power to the Court to condone the delay.</u>

25. It has been submitted on behalf of the respondent No.1 that the appellant was a trustee in respect of the Bills of Exchange and so in terms of the principle laid down in 12 DLR 10, the question of limitation will not arise in the present case. However to attract section 10 of the Limitation Act, as held in 12 DLR 10, there must be vesting of property in the appellant in trust for a specific purpose but in the present case there is no such vesting not to speck of any specific purpose. In the decision reported in 12 DLR 10, the defendant insisted that the full amount of money must be paid to them before they parted with the goods and accordingly the plaintiff, in order to have the released, paid the full amount under protest saying that they would claim refund of any amount that might be found due from the defendants to the plaintiff and in the suit the plaintiff claimed the excess amount which was due to him on the ground that defendants held it was trust for him and it was held that the aforesaid payment under protest would be sufficient to constitute trust for specific purpose within the meaning under section 10 of the Limitation Act. But in the applications (plaints) of the present suits it has merely been stated that the appellant "accepted for honor" the said 9 bills of Exchange drawn against the letter of credit in question and the appellant having not given notice of dishonor nor caused to be noted protest for dishonor by non acceptance or by non payment of any of the said bills continue to remain to be holder without consideration of the said Bills but as stated earlier the respondent No.1 during 1985-87 drew the said Bills of Exchange for total sum of Tk. 102,70,000.00 on BADC and not on the appellant and so how subsequent Bills of Exchange for Tk. 99,05,35,167.00 could be drawn on 15.9.97 and 25.9.97 in the name of the appellant? However in the concise statement for the first tie that it has been stated that from the Statement of Account dated 11.3.99 it will be evident that the appellant having collected payments on the 9 Bills drawn on BADC during 1985-87 is a trustee but as stated earlier the letter dated 18.9.97 and certificate of BADC dated 13.12.88, on which the respondent No. 1 relied for the cause of actions for the present suits, show that out of total bill amount of Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 a sum of Tk. 85,28,372.32 was paid to the respondent No.1 and a sum of Tk. 17,41,627.68 was deducted by BADC as penalty etc. as per terms of the contract over which litigation is pending Moreover in the applications (plaints ) of the suits, there is no mentioned of the above statement of Account dated 11.3 and the same has also not been furnished in the paper book four our perusal. However, such issue, if any may be decided in the suits.

26. It also appears that a Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing by judgment and order dated 4.5.2002 already discharged the Rule issued in Civil Revision No. 10 of 1987 holding that-

"Article 159 of the limitation Act prescribes for a period of 10 days from the date of service of summons. Record shows the summons was served on the defendant Bank on 19.8.98 and 28.8.98 was fixed for appearance Mr. Khan showed us that 28.8.98 and 29.8.98 were both closed holidays. Section 4 of the limitation Act provides, where the period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application expires on a day when the Court is closed the suit appeal or application may be instituted preferred or made on the day the reopens. So the application made for leave under order 37 rule (2) and (3) of the Code on 30.8.98 cannot be held to be out of time of the period of limitation of 10 days. The teamed District Judge therefore has not committed any error either of law or procedure in entertaining such application for leave. The teamed District Judge on consideration of the application and the record has come to a finding that there was a tribal issue raised and the defendant should be allowed to defend the suit. Upon such finding, learned district Judge granted leave to the defendant Bank to appear and defend the suit."

27. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division made the Rule absolute just within 28 days without at all considering that in the present suits the respondent No.1 prayed for decree for Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 with further interest and compensation on the decrial amount and the above amount of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 was claimed on the basis of the Bills drawn during the years 1985-87 on BADC for total Tk. 1,02,70,000.00 out of which TK. 85,28,372.32 was paid by BADC deducting only Tk. 17,41,627.69 as penalty etc. over which the respondent No. 1 initiated proceeding which is pending for hearing and the High Court Division, also did not conciser that out of Tk. 99,05,35, 187.00 as above, an amount of Tk. 79,24,92,446.00 was claimed as compensation under section 117 of the Act though in terms of Rule; 2(2)(a) of Order 37 CPC in such summery proceedings, the plaintiff can only claim interest under section 79 or 80 of the Act and that in view of making the rule absolute the court will have no other option but to pass exparte decree for Tk. 99.05.35.187.00 along with further interest and compensation   under section 117 of the Act as claimed from the date of the decree and as it appears from the contents of order dated 19.7.98 of the District Court, no court fee has been paid on the claim of Tk. 99,05,35,187.00 as yet. It also appears that the respondent No. 1 filed the above writ petition suppressing the fact that at their instance Rule has been issued in Civil Revision No. 10 of 1987 on the same issue by the High Court Division and the same was pending for hearing. As stated earlier, in the meanwhile above Rule was discharged. Further, it also appears that in the writ petition petitioner prayed for issuing Rule upon the Presiding Judge of the court instead of the person who was going to be affected and the High Court Division just on the basis of the prayer of the respondent No.1, issued Rule only on the Presiding Judge, District Court Dhaka who as per usual practice, did not appear and taking advantage of the same, the respondent No.1 got the Rule absolute depriving the appellant to bring on record the relevant facts.

28. In 44 DLR 490 relied on by the respondent No.1 the High Court Division held that in such summery suits Article 159 of the Limitation Act was applicable and accordingly sent the case records back to the trial Court after setting aside the order passed by the trial Court granting leave. But as it appears in the suit in question the defendant appeared on 23.11.88 in response to the summons and merely filed an application praying for time to file written statement and did not at all file an application supported by an affidavit praying for leave and the order of the Court passed on that date allowing the defendant to file written statement on 07.12.88 which resulted in filing of an application by the plaintiff on 5.12.1998 under section 1521 C.P.C praying for vacating the order passed on 23.11.88 on the ground that in the absence of prior leave obtained by the defendant to appear that in the absence of prior leave obtained by the defendant to appear and defend the suit, the order dated 23.11.88 was erroneous in law. However in the present cases on 26.08.99 the appellant entered appearance and prayed for time for filing written statement but on 30.8.98 the appellant also filed another application supported by an affidavit praying for leave to appeal and defend the suits.

29. Moreover, in the present case, the learned District Judge without at all considering that 28.8.98 and 29.8.98 being holidays, the application dated 30.8.98 was within 10 days condoned the delay referring to the case of Srinivasan Vs. Bhakthavatsulu Naidu, reported in AIR 1953 Madras 909 and then granted leave holding that there was triable issue. But in the writ petition the High Court Division considering that 28.8.98 and 29.8.98 being holidays held that the application dated 30.8.98 was within time but made the Rule absolute holding that the above application did not disclose facts of triable issue. As it appears the respondent No.1 did not file any leave petition challenging the above finding of the High Court Division that application dated 30.8.98 was within time but raised this issue of limitation in the concise statement and also made submission on this point of limitation without obtaining any leave. However we have already answered this question of limitation.

30. Regarding the submission of Mr. M. S. Khan that the information slip shows that the application filed by the appellant Bank on 30.8.98 were not under Rule 3 of Order 37 CPC it appears that in the above applications the appellant specifically prayed for leave to appeal and defend the suits and so the said applications are certainly applications under Rule 3(1) for obtaining leave from the court to appear and defend the suit the defendant has to file an application under Rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC.

31. Accordingly the appeal is allowed and the judgment and order dated 21.8.2000 passed in Writ petition No. 3869 of 2000 is set aside with costs.

32. The observations made above are only for resolving the issue as to whether leave was granted in accordance with law and the same will have no bearing on the merits of the pending suits. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Ministry of Law as well to the Law Commission for consideration as to whether necessary amendment is required to be made in Rule 3(1) of Order 37 CPC as made in the said provision in different country/countries providing scope for condonation of delay.

End.
